Leon grimaced, pulling in a slow breath as the room tilted slightly. “You can’t... stay here,” he warned, voice strained, slurred around the edges, but firmer now. “He’s trying t’ draw you out.” Meg didn’t let go. “We’re not leaving you here to get shocked into a stroke. This thing’s gotta give eventually.” Claudette was still at his side, gently adjusting the way his arm hung from the cuff. “Can you move your fingers?” she asked urgently. “I need to check if—” Leon’s breathing hitched. His head slumped back against the cabinet with a dull clunk , eyelids fluttering as he tried to blink back the gray that teased the edges of his vision. He forced the words out through a tight jaw. “Get... out. B’fore he comes back.” Claudette glanced up at Meg, then back to Leon, frustrated. “We can’t just— damn it, you’re destabilizing. He’s burning your nerves. You’re already spasming.” Leon shoved lightly at Meg’s leg with his free hand, trying to push her back. He shook off some more of the creeping sparks around his vision and forced his voice to steady. He had to get them out of the area, and they weren’t going to leave if they thought he was collapsing into himself. “Look. Jake’s hunting the keys. He’ll get me loose. But you two need to go .” He exhaled hard, trying to will his body still. “Last thing we need is a daisy chain of survivors getting fried one by one.” He looked at them both, gaze sharp despite the haze settling over him. “Get back to the campfire. I’ll make it there... eventually. ” Claudette sat back on her heels, flexing her fingers into her lap like she couldn’t decide whether to reach for Leon again or just do something . Anything. But there wasn’t much left to do. He was already in rough shape — when they had come in, he barely looked like he recognized where he was — and Herman wasn’t easing off. If anything, his cruelty was escalating. Dragging this out. Making a point. Moving on was really the only logical choice. Plus, matter how bad it got, eventually the Fog WOULD bring him back to the campfire. ...Whatever was left of him, anyways. Claudette’s gaze lingered on the doorway. Her gut screamed that walking away was wrong — but logic didn’t leave room for better options. “I don’t want to just...” she started, then swallowed hard, looking up at Meg. “But if we don’t go, he’s going to make it worse.” Meg kicked away from the cabinet with a frustrated cry. She’d known from the moment they’d walked in that Leon had already accepted this outcome. He was never expecting them to get him out. Just to go . To leave. To not get added to the roster of broken bodies littering the map. It burned. But that chain was stronger than she was, and the longer they stayed there, the greater the chance of the Doctor finding them and adding them to the collection. She swore, dragging a palm down her face before stepping over to help Claudette back to her feet. “You better be right about Jake,” she muttered tightly. Leon’s head lolled slightly to the side, and he gave a lopsided, tired half-smile. “I usually am.” The lights above them flickered — a soft static pulse that passed overhead like the distant tail of a storm. Both women turned and slipped through the doorway, their footsteps retreating fast into the hall. For a few seconds, the room held still. Then Leon exhaled — slow and shaky — as if holding his breath had been the only thing keeping him upright this long. He slumped back against the cabinet, legs unfolding out of their cramped brace. The shift made the cuff pull tight again, dragging his arm upward until the nerves sparked. He closed his eyes, willing back the nausea from how badly the room kept tilting as he tried to breathe through it. It wasn’t much — his ribs ached too much to fill fully, and his lungs felt crackled at the edges — but at least he didn’t have to hold it steady for someone else’s sake. The stillness wasn’t peace. It was just the absence of people he had to lie to. His free hand twitched on the floor beside him, fingers curling slightly before losing strength and going still. One shoulder hitched in a delayed shiver — his body still trying to process the last blast as if it hadn’t registered yet that it was over. He knew what muscle fatigue looked like. He’d studied shock trauma, nerve damage, all of it. He knew exactly what signs were setting in now. He just didn’t know how many more he could take. He tilted his head back against the cabinet, eyes drifting up to the chain above. “...Better be close, Jake,” Jake was close. He was loaded down with junk—twisted bedframe scraps, broken IV stands, a section of handrail yanked off the wall with sheer panic-strength. Anything that looked solid enough to break open wood was fair game now. Subtlety had left the building six shocks ago. It clattered noisily as he staggered back through the empty doorframe of the Doctor’s office, dumping the pile at his feet like a desperate scavenger at a workbench. The hallway lights above him flickered. A scream echoed faintly from somewhere behind the walls. It didn’t sound like the first ones. This one was shorter. Rougher. Jake’s face tightened, jaw clenching so hard it hurt. “Son of a bitch,” he muttered, grabbing a chunk of rail that looked fairly sharp on one end. “Just hang in there...” He dropped to his knees beside the locked desk drawer again, wedging the metal between the seam.
